text: SOUTH KOREA'S LEVERAGE FEVER: WHY SO MANY PEOPLE BORROW TO INVEST English translation of the provided Vietnamese video transcript When
people think of South Korea, they often think of kimchi, romantic dramas, and youthful-looking oppas. But there is another issue that
has become an increasingly serious headache: more and more people believe that investing is no longer about building wealth slowly over
time. Instead, they see it as the quickest way to transform their lives. Stocks, cryptocurrencies, real estate—anything with the potential
to rise in price attracts people eager to jump in. And what makes this game so much more dangerous is margin
or, more simply, borrowed money used for investing. The consequences became clear in early 2026, when South Korea's KOSPI index plunged
by more than 18% in just a few days, wiping hundreds of billions of dollars off the market—one of its
sharpest declines in years. What stood out, however, was that many investors were using extremely high leverage. Some securities firms even
had to temporarily suspend margin lending because they had reached their lending limits. But why did this happen in a market
that is far from an emerging one? South Korea is one of Asia's largest economies. It has weathered numerous financial crises
and its people are famous for being competitive and disciplined in their work. So why are so many people willing to
borrow money to bet on the market? And why has leverage become so popular? That's what we're going to explore in
today's video. I'm Nheo, and this is the story of South Korea's leverage fever. First, we need to understand what leverage
or margin trading—actually is. Let's have a quick refresher. Margin trading, simply put, means borrowing money from a brokerage to
buy additional shares. Say you have 100 million Vietnamese dong, and the brokerage lends you another 100 million. Instead of buying
100 million dong worth of stocks, you can now buy 200 million dong worth. If the share price rises by
10%, you make about 20 million dong rather than 10 million. That's the basic idea. But borrowing money does not guarantee
that the market will rise. If the shares fall by 10%, your loss is also doubled. Meanwhile, you still have to
repay the loan, along with all the interest. In a way, margin trading is like fitting a racing engine to your
investment portfolio. If you're heading in the right direction, it's fantastic. But one sharp turn can send you flying off the
